sentences.text: At a rally in Montana this October, President Trump told the crowd, "we have very little inflation".
On CBS News, a politics reporter put it the other way: "inflation is higher than when he took office".
Very little, or more than before? Let's put both claims against the government's own price index.
Start with the boldest version: Trump has also said, flatly, "we don't have inflation".
The Bureau of Labor Statistics' September report says otherwise: consumer prices were 3.7 percent higher than a year earlier, and still rising month to month.
So there is inflation. The real argument is whether it's high, and that depends on what you compare it with.
Trump's comparison is the past: "we inherited the worst inflation in history", he told the Montana rally.
These figures can't rank all of history, but the 2022 peak was real: in June 2022 the yearly rate hit 9.1 percent, and today's is less than half of that.
And early this year, the low-inflation case was strong. Of January's reading, the YouTube channel The Right-Wing Populist said it was "the lowest we've had in five years".
Close enough: the January rate was 2.4 percent, a whisker above the lowest reading since March 2021 and about the pace of early 2020 just before the pandemic.
By September, that case had gone: the yearly rate was higher than in any month of 2024 or 2025.
It was also above the 3.0 percent of January 2025 (the month the administration took office): what he actually inherited, and the comparison CBS was making.
Trump has a shorter window in mind: "we're at 1.7% inflation for the last three months", he told reporters.
The index says otherwise: from June to September, the seasonally adjusted index ran at a pace of about 4.6 percent a year.
To be fair, slide that window back one month, to end in August, and the pace drops to about 0.2 percent a year, because prices fell in June.
Pick your window, and you pick your answer.
The Federal Reserve, for its part, said at its September press conference that "for more than five years, inflation has been running above target".
Its stated goal is 2 percent, and its own officials expect 3.7 percent over 2026 on the price index they forecast, called PCE, short for personal consumption expenditures.
On the consumer price index, the yearly rate hasn't dropped below 2.3 percent in any month with a reading since March 2021.
And if the rate does come down, will prices?
Even The Right-Wing Populist says not: "prices are technically expanding, but the actual rate is decreasing".
That's what happened after the peak: from January 2023 to September 2024, the yearly rate fell from 6.4 percent to 2.4, while the price level itself rose about 5.4 percent.
So inflation is not gone, and it is not at its peak. Which leaves the next question: what is pushing it up?
The rate had been easing into the new year; then, from March to May, it climbed to 3.3, 3.8 and 4.2 percent.
NBC News said the economy had been "heading towards that number earlier this year", the Fed's target, "but then with the Iran war prices shot up".
The price tables confirm the jump, but they don't say what caused it.

One line in them stands out, though: gasoline's own index leapt 24.9 percent in March alone and kept rising through May before falling back in June, but the tables don't say how much of the overall jump that explains.
September's report is more specific: gasoline rose 9.1 percent in that one month and accounted for over half of the month's whole rise.
But an economist on PBS NewsHour pointed out that "the war in Iran is not causing medical care, dental care, toys, apparel".
The report agrees that it isn't only fuel: used cars, airline fares, medical care and apparel all went up in September.
But the spread is modest: prices outside food and energy, called core, rose 0.3 percent on the month, no faster than in August, and 2.6 percent over the year.
Some economists think the underlying rate is higher. "I think underlying inflation is around 3%", Michael Strain said in June.
Core has run a little under that all year, between 2.4 and 2.9 percent, and it had slowed from 3.1 percent in the summer of 2025 before ticking back up.
Housing runs hotter: the shelter index rose 3.2 percent over the year.
And tariffs? Economists at the New York Fed estimate they added around 2.9 percentage points to price growth for the goods they studied, by February 2026.
They caution that it measures those goods against less-exposed ones, so the number is illustrative, and it doesn't tell us how much of overall inflation tariffs explain.
So in September the biggest single push was gasoline, while core sat a little under Strain's figure, with housing above it.
The people quoted here mostly weren't arguing about the numbers; they were arguing about the yardstick.
So when someone tells you inflation is high or low, ask: compared with what, and over which months?
And when you hear the rate is falling, check core, and remember that a slower rate still means prices that are climbing.
